rows.text: An Arctic Satellite Broadband Mission spacecraft. Geostationary satellites sit over the equator, so above roughly 75° North they are below the horizon and there is no broadband at all — which is why Space Norway put ASBM-1 and ASBM-2 into a highly elliptical three-apogee orbit, 8,100 km at perigee and 43,500 km at apogee, inclined 63° and phased so that one of the pair is always dwelling over the north. They carry payloads for the Norwegian Armed Forces, the U.S. Space Force and the commercial operator Viasat, and the American EPS-R payload was the first operational U.S. Department of Defense payload ever hosted on a foreign spacecraft. For anyone planning operations above the Arctic Circle this is the communications architecture that makes them possible. A spacecraft can be owned and operated by one organisation and still carry, or be contracted to serve, another organisation's mission. Operated by Space Norway, this spacecraft also carries a payload for the Enhanced Polar System - Recapitalization (EPS-R), sponsored by the U.S. Space Force. The manufacturer describes a secure payload interface that completely isolates this payload from the rest of the satellite - one spacecraft, but the tenants cannot reach each other. Published by Northrop Grumman, the spacecraft's manufacturer. It also carries the European Commission Arctic radiation monitoring instrument as a guest payload, sponsored by the European Commission. A fourth tenant on the same two spacecraft: a small scientific instrument sharing a ride with two nations' military communications and a commercial broadband payload, and measuring the very radiation belts this site draws elsewhere. Published by Space Norway, the spacecraft's owner. It also carries a payload for Norwegian Armed Forces Arctic X-band communications, sponsored by the Norwegian Armed Forces. Space Norway states that these two satellites host payloads for the Norwegian Armed Forces, the U.S. Space Force and a commercial operator at the same time, which is why the catalog's single owner field cannot describe them. Published by Space Norway, the spacecraft's owner. It also carries a payload for Viasat Arctic Ka-band broadband, sponsored by Viasat. Space Norway describes the commercial Ka-band payload as the largest aboard the spacecraft, so the biggest tenant here is neither of the two militaries also on board. Published by Space Norway, the spacecraft's owner.

A GPS satellite. NAVSTAR is the Global Positioning System's own programme designation, which is why the best-known constellation in orbit is catalogued under a name most people never see. The U.S. Space Force's 2nd Space Operations Squadron flies it as at least 24 slots in six equally spaced orbital planes at about 20,200 km, each satellite circling the Earth twice a day, with several extra spacecraft aloft so that coverage survives maintenance and decommissioning. For a maritime operator the point to hold onto is that this is a one-way broadcast of very weak signals from 20,000 km away: it is jammable and spoofable close to a contested coast, and most of what separates one satellite generation from the next is the effort to answer that. GPS III — built by Lockheed Martin, first launched in 2018 — adds the fourth civil signal L1C, designed to be interoperable with Europe's Galileo, has no Selective Availability capability at all, and is built for a 15-year life. This one is GPS III flight 1, named “Vespucci”, space vehicle number SVN 74, broadcasting pseudo-random-noise code PRN 04 in plane F, slot 4 of the constellation. It is the first GPS III spacecraft. A spacecraft can be owned and operated by one organisation and still carry, or be contracted to serve, another organisation's mission. Operated by U.S. Space Force, this spacecraft also carries a payload for the U.S. Nuclear Detonation Detection System (USNDS), sponsored by the National Nuclear Security Administration, U.S. Department of Energy. The navigation satellite you use to find your way is also a detonation detector for a different department of government: the Department of Energy pays for the sensors and builds them at Sandia and Los Alamos, and the Space Force flies them. Sandia records a current block of eight detection systems whose last unit launched on 30 May 2025, and the site attaches the programme to exactly those eight navigation satellites - the eighth of which is the one the registry shows launching that day - rather than to the whole constellation. Published by Sandia National Laboratories.

A Shijian (实践, shíjiàn — "practice", in the sense of putting something into practice) spacecraft, catalogued under the abbreviation SJ. Fifty have launched since 1971, and it is the single most misread family in the Chinese catalogue, because it genuinely contains both ends of the spectrum: Shijian-10 was a recoverable microgravity and life-science capsule that ran 472 experiments for the Chinese Academy of Sciences, Shijian-13 flies commercially as ChinaSat-16 carrying twenty-six Ka-band beams for China Satcom, and Shijian-17, -21 and -25 have conducted the geostationary proximity operations that US Space Command has publicly described as a counterspace concern. The US Air Force's China Aerospace Studies Institute assesses that Shijian sits later in China's development pipeline than Shiyan — establishing operational practice for systems already adopted, rather than piloting new ones. Xinhua's standard announcement is that a Shijian satellite is "mainly used for space environment detection and related technology verification"; the Jamestown Foundation assesses the programme as deliberately dual-use and treats the absence of published operational data as itself indicative. This site names no mission for the family as a whole, because the family does not have one. Two sub-series are separately assessed: Gunter Krebs reads the ten Shijian-6 spacecraft, flown in pairs, as possibly carrying electronic intelligence payloads, and the US Space Force states plainly that they are believed to have a signals intelligence mission; Krebs labels his own reading of the eight Shijian-11 satellites explicitly as speculation, which is the standard this site tries to match.

A Yunhai-1 (云海一号, "sea of clouds") spacecraft. Xinhua's description is that it is used for atmospheric and marine environment surveys, space environment surveys, disaster prevention and scientific experiments; the spacecraft are built by the Shanghai Academy of Spaceflight Technology, part of CASC. What China does not say is who the customer is, and two independent bodies say it is the military: the WMO's own OSCAR satellite database states that CNSA operates the Yunhai system for the Chinese military, and Henk Smid, writing in ROOM Space Journal, assesses the series as military meteorology whose data complements the civil Fengyun satellites. That is an assessment, not a Chinese statement, and this site records it as one. The practical signature is consistent with it: no Yunhai satellite has a WMO station identifier, no instrument list has ever been published for any of them, and the OSCAR record carries no data-access link at all — a meteorological system that does not exchange its data is not behaving like a civil one. Yunhai-1 satellites fly sun-synchronous orbits near 780 km. Yunhai 1-02 was struck by orbital debris in 2021, which Jonathan McDowell identified as the first major confirmed orbital collision since 2009. This attribution is contested: Xinhua, for the Chinese state characterises it as a satellite for atmospheric and marine environment survey, space environment survey, disaster prevention and scientific experiment, while the WMO's OSCAR database and the analyst Henk Smid assesses it as a military meteorological satellite. This site records the assessment by the WMO's OSCAR database and the analyst Henk Smid and shows both readings.

One of four Ludi Kancha Weixing (陆地勘查卫星, "land survey satellite") spacecraft, launched one at a time between December 2017 and March 2018. Xinhua's description of each was a single sentence — the satellite is mainly used for remote sensing exploration of land resources — and CASC identified the builder as DFH Satellite, under its Fifth Academy. Everything else is assessment, and it is unusually convergent. Gunter Krebs records them as very-high-resolution imaging satellites likely intended for military purposes; Henk Smid, writing in ROOM Space Journal, notes that the secrecy is extreme even by Chinese standards and reads the four-launches-in-four-months cadence as a pattern previously seen only in military programmes; Rui Barbosa assesses that the generic designation is a cover of the same kind China has used for Yaogan, related to CAST's second-generation electro-optical reconnaissance satellites; and Jonathan McDowell's GCAT codes the operator as a PLA entity. No Chinese organisation has ever been named as the user of the imagery. A ground resolution figure of about 0.7 m circulates: it is Smid's estimate inferred from the spacecraft's external shape, not a published specification, and should be treated as such. No image of an LKW satellite has ever been released. This attribution is contested: Xinhua and the Chinese State Council characterises it as remote sensing exploration of land resources, while Gunter Krebs, Henk Smid and Jonathan McDowell's GCAT assesses it as military topographic reconnaissance. This site records the assessment by Gunter Krebs, Henk Smid and Jonathan McDowell's GCAT and shows both readings.

A satellite in the Tianmu-1 (天目一号) radio-occultation weather constellation — the one Chinese commercial constellation whose data has been accepted into China's operational numerical weather prediction system. Each 55 kg spacecraft carries a GNSS occultation sounder and a reflectometry receiver working across BeiDou, GPS, Galileo and GLONASS. Radio occultation works by watching a navigation satellite set through the limb of the atmosphere and inverting the bending of the ray path, which yields temperature, humidity and pressure profiles with no radiometric calibration drift — the property that makes occultation an anchor for reanalysis. The reflectometry channel adds sea surface wind speed, sea ice and soil moisture. On 30 December 2024 the China Meteorological Administration admitted 23 Tianmu-1 satellites and 12 Yunyao-1 satellites into its operational observing system, the first time commercial smallsat data had been accepted there; the constellation currently returns about 30,000 profiles a day against a stated 90,000 at completion, and its profiles feed the GRAPES forecast model. The operator is a subsidiary of CASIC, a state-owned defence and aerospace conglomerate that the US Department of Defense lists as a Chinese military company — that relationship is one of ownership, and no source states a military use of the occultation data itself. This one flies the sun-synchronous business sub-constellation, published at about 520 km and 97.4 degrees; the low-inclination sub-constellation that would fill in tropical sampling is still planned rather than flown.

A Yunhai-2 (云海二号) spacecraft, flown in batches of six. The WMO's OSCAR database records the Yunhai programme as operated by CNSA for the Chinese military and describes Yunhai-2 as a twelve-satellite GNSS radio-occultation constellation whose main mission is temperature and humidity sounding with a substantial contribution to space weather; Gunter Krebs and Henk Smid read it the same way. All of that is assessment: China has published no instrument list for any Yunhai-2 satellite, and this site does not present the occultation payload as an established fact. If the assessment is right, these spacecraft do the same physics as the commercial Tianmu-1 and Yunyao-1 constellations — watching navigation satellites set through the atmospheric limb and inverting the ray bending into profiles — for a customer that does not share the output. The orbital history is genuinely odd and worth knowing: the first six were inserted in 2018 into two separate shells, three near 520 km and three near 1,095 km, and during mid-2019 all six manoeuvred into roughly circular 800 km orbits, one group climbing and the other descending. This attribution is contested: Xinhua, for the Chinese state characterises it as a satellite for atmospheric and marine environment survey, space environment survey, disaster prevention and scientific experiment, while the WMO's OSCAR database, Gunter Krebs and Henk Smid assesses it as a military GNSS radio-occultation weather constellation. This site records the assessment by the WMO's OSCAR database, Gunter Krebs and Henk Smid and shows both readings.

For a maritime operator the point to hold onto is that this is a one-way broadcast of very weak signals from 20,000 km away: it is jammable and spoofable close to a contested coast, and most of what separates one satellite generation from the next is the effort to answer that. Block IIR-M — “modernised”, launched between 2005 and 2009 — added the second civil signal L2C and the military M-code, the jam-resistant signal with flexible transmit power that makes GPS usable in an electronic-warfare environment. This one is Block IIR-M flight 7, space vehicle number SVN 49. SVN 49 is the exception in the constellation. It carried the demonstration payload that let the United States meet an ITU deadline for the L5 band, but the way that payload was grafted on left signal leakage reflecting off the L5 filter and re-transmitting about 30 nanoseconds late — a self-inflicted multipath that showed up as elevation-dependent pseudorange residuals at the monitor stations. It has never been set healthy for routine navigation service and is held in reserve, which is why it carries no plane or slot assignment.

A satellite in CentiSpace (微厘空间, "micro-centimetre space" — the name states the accuracy goal), a Chinese low-Earth-orbit navigation augmentation constellation operated by Beijing Future Navigation Technology. It does not replace BeiDou or GPS: it broadcasts precise ephemeris and satellite-clock corrections on two dedicated L-band signals, CL1 at 1569–1581 MHz and CL5 at 1170–1182 MHz, both BPSK at 2.046 Mcps, and it also monitors GNSS integrity. The operator's target, published to the UN's International Committee on GNSS, is sub-50 cm from a cold start in 5 seconds and sub-10 cm in a minute — the value of a LEO layer is that its fast geometry change collapses the convergence time that makes conventional precise point positioning slow. The published design is three sub-constellations: Walker 120/12/1 at 975 km and 55 degrees, Walker 30/3/1 at 1,100 km and 87.4 degrees, and Walker 40/4/1 at 1,100 km and 30 degrees. Two things an operator should carry: the spacecraft in orbit today are measurably lower than that published design, and the constellation size is stated variously as 120, 160, 190 and 240 by different Chinese sources. SpaceNews reports that CETC — a state defence electronics conglomerate — is involved and that the BeiDou Industry Fund is an investor; the operating company itself is not named on any US government military-company list. This one flies the inclined shell the operator published as Walker 120/12/1 at 55 degrees — the design choice that concentrates the augmentation over mid and low latitudes rather than over the poles.

A satellite in Guowang (国网, "national network"), China's state low-Earth-orbit broadband constellation. Space-track catalogues these spacecraft under the Chinese series name Hulianwang Digui — "internet, low orbit" — which is why they do not appear under the programme name a reader would search for. The operator is China Satellite Network Group (China SatNet), a state-owned enterprise created in April 2021 and placed directly under SASAC, the body that supervises China's largest state firms; the spacecraft come from several contractors, among them CAST and Galaxy Space. The published architecture is 12,992 satellites — roughly 6,080 between 500 and 600 km and 6,912 near 1,145 km — with ITU spectrum filings made in late 2020 under the designation GW. Chinese accounts describe a bus able to carry broadband, laser-communication, synthetic-aperture-radar and optical remote-sensing payloads rather than a single communications payload, which is why analysts read Guowang as strategic national infrastructure and not only as a consumer broadband service. What is not published is the part an operator would most want: no mass, no dimensions, no power budget and no capability description has been released for any Guowang flight, so treat any specific capability claim about an individual spacecraft as unsourced. This one flies in the mid-inclination shell, which China publishes as 50.0 degrees inclination at about 1,156 km; a spacecraft measured well below that figure is still raising its orbit.

A Huanjing (环境减灾, "environment and disaster reduction") spacecraft in China's Environmental Protection and Disaster Monitoring Constellation, operated by CRESDA for the Ministry of Ecology and Environment and the Ministry of Emergency Management. This is the one large Chinese Earth-observation family in this partition with a working public data portal and no military attribution from any named analyst. The second generation completed a declared "2+2" constellation — two optical and two radar. HJ-2A and HJ-2B fly at 650 km sun-synchronous with a 10:30 descending node and carry a 16 m four-band wide-view camera built from four stitched CCD cameras, an infrared camera, a hyperspectral imager and an atmospheric corrector that samples the same field of view for radiometric correction; sources disagree on the wide-view resolution, with ESA's eoPortal saying 30 m against 16 m from the manufacturer, the WMO and China's own environment ministry, and this site follows the three Chinese-side sources. HJ-2E and HJ-2F carry an S-band synthetic aperture radar at 2.7 GHz instead, switchable between 5 m over 35 km and 25 m over 100 km, plus an on-board emergency processor that extracts hot-spot information in flight to shorten the response time on marine oil spills; they fly dawn-dusk orbits near 500 km. The first generation, HJ-1A and HJ-1B, dates from 2008. ESA credits the constellation with climate variables including ocean colour, sea-ice cover and thickness, snow cover and soil moisture.

A satellite in the Yunyao-1 (云遥一号) commercial weather constellation, built and operated by Tianjin Yunyao Aerospace Technology — a genuinely private Chinese company, which Xinhua describes as such. Each 30–35 kg spacecraft carries one combined instrument doing both GNSS radio occultation and GNSS reflectometry: a 3×1 antenna array watching navigation satellites set through the atmospheric limb for temperature, humidity and ionospheric profiles, and a 4×5 array collecting forward-scattered signal off the surface for winds, soil moisture and ice. The published design is 90 satellites in 18 planes — twelve sun-synchronous planes of six at 535 km and 97.5 degrees, six low-inclination planes of three at 500, 600 and 800 km and 50 degrees — the low-inclination planes existing specifically to sample the tropics, which a purely polar constellation samples worst. China states the purpose plainly: substitution for foreign occultation data, and a forecast product for Belt and Road partner countries. Yunyao data entered the China Meteorological Administration's operational system alongside Tianmu-1 on 30 December 2024. The programme has lost nine satellites to launch failures. English Wikipedia attributes Yunyao-1 to Chang Guang Satellite Technology; every Chinese and primary source attributes it to Tianjin Yunyao, and this site follows the primary sources. This one flies one of the six low-inclination planes at 50 degrees, the part of the design that exists to sample the tropics.

A satellite in the Tianqi constellation (天启星座), China's first low-Earth-orbit satellite Internet-of-Things network to reach operational service. It is built and run by Beijing Guodian Gaoke Technology, a private company, and it is deliberately not a broadband system: the payload is a UHF narrowband store-and-forward relay carrying short text, voice clips and small images, engineered so that a ground terminal can close the link on 100–500 mW. The published design is 38 satellites — 36 at 900 km and 45 degrees inclination in six planes of six, plus two in sun-synchronous orbit — sized to cover the maritime, polar and interior gaps that terrestrial cellular does not reach. Chinese state media put the operating fleet at 41. In May 2026 the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology granted Guodian Gaoke China's first two-year commercial trial licence for satellite IoT operations, and the company has signed distribution agreements in South Africa and Malaysia. Later ITU filings would expand the system substantially, to 3,918 or 1,132 satellites depending on which filing is live. No named source associates Tianqi with the Chinese military, and the operator's cited users are forestry, agriculture, aquaculture, petroleum and emergency response. This one flies well below the published 900 km / 45-degree operational shell — the early Tianqi flights took the orbits their rideshare launches offered, and no source states which of them are in operational service.

A Haiyang-2 (海洋二号) ocean dynamics satellite, and the most operationally useful Chinese spacecraft in this catalogue for a METOC watch floor. The payload measures the sea surface rather than looking at it: a dual-frequency radar altimeter at 13.58 GHz Ku-band and 5.25 GHz C-band for sea surface height and significant wave height, a 13.256 GHz Ku-band scatterometer for ocean surface vector winds, and — on HY-2B only — a five-frequency microwave radiometer from 6.6 to 37 GHz for sea surface temperature, water vapour and cloud liquid water. NSOAS publishes the accuracies: about 5 cm on sea surface height, 2 m/s or 10 per cent on wind speed, 20 degrees on wind direction, 0.5 m or 10 per cent on significant wave height. HY-2A and HY-2B fly sun-synchronous with a 06:00 descending node and a dual 14-day and 168-day repeat; HY-2C and HY-2D deliberately do not, sitting at 66 degrees inclination in drifting orbits, which is what cut sea-surface-wind revisit over more than 80 per cent of the world's oceans from about twelve hours to six. The scatterometers return roughly 180,000 wind vectors a day, and — uniquely in this partition — the data reaches Western operational meteorology: EUMETSAT's OSI SAF has distributed HY-2B/C/D scatterometer winds on EUMETCast since 31 October 2024, processed by KNMI. NSOAS also states national defence construction among the system's purposes in its own words, so the dual-use reading here does not require an outside analyst.

A Hulianwang Jishu Shiyan (卫星互联网技术试验卫星) spacecraft — a satellite-internet technology test satellite. Despite the three shared letters this has nothing to do with the civil Huanjing environment and disaster satellites catalogued as HJ; the two programmes are unrelated. China describes these as conducting technology verification for direct broadband connection from handsets to satellites and for the integration of space and terrestrial networks. Gunter Krebs and SpaceNews both assess them as pathfinders for Guowang, China's state LEO broadband megaconstellation, though SpaceNews is careful to note they could equally be unrelated or serve several projects; their orbits are consistent with the Guowang shells. They are not one design. CASC's Fifth Academy built the first pair, and later batches came from the Shanghai Academy of Spaceflight Technology, the Chinese Academy of Sciences' microsatellite institute, and the commercial firms Chang Guang Satellite Technology and Galaxy Space. One documented oddity is worth an operator's attention: on three of the first four launches, Chinese announcements stated fewer satellites than were subsequently catalogued — Xinhua described one launch as carrying "a satellite" and two entered orbit. Across this whole partition that is the only case where China's public account is demonstrably contradicted rather than merely incomplete. Nothing has been published about the spacecraft's mass, payload or appearance.

A satellite in Jilin-1 (吉林一号), China's largest commercial optical imaging constellation, named for the province where its operator sits. Chang Guang Satellite Technology is a 2014 spin-out of the Changchun Institute of Optics, Fine Mechanics and Physics — a Chinese Academy of Sciences institute — with the Jilin provincial government among its shareholders, so it is commercial in form and state-derived in origin. The catalogue name says which camera is aboard: Gaofen ("high resolution") satellites are roughly 40 kg spacecraft returning 0.75 m panchromatic and 3 m multispectral imagery on a swath of tens of kilometres from about 535 km; Kuanfu ("wide swath") satellites trade nothing away and instead widen the field, the 01B spacecraft imaging at 0.5 m panchromatic and 2 m multispectral across more than 150 km. The company's stated plan is 138 satellites as a first phase, expanding to 300, with a target of imaging any point on Earth 23 to 25 times a day. Imagery is sold, not exchanged: the WMO record for Jilin-1 carries a sales contact where other systems carry a data link. In December 2023 the US Treasury designated Chang Guang Satellite Technology for supplying high-resolution imagery to the Wagner Group, and Gunter's Space Page records two Gaofen-03D spacecraft as having been sold to Wagner outright — a commercial Chinese constellation is not thereby a military one, but its imagery has demonstrably reached a combatant.

A satellite in Guowang (国网, "national network"), China's state low-Earth-orbit broadband constellation. Space-track catalogues these spacecraft under the Chinese series name Hulianwang Digui — "internet, low orbit" — which is why they do not appear under the programme name a reader would search for. The operator is China Satellite Network Group (China SatNet), a state-owned enterprise created in April 2021 and placed directly under SASAC, the body that supervises China's largest state firms; the spacecraft come from several contractors, among them CAST and Galaxy Space. The published architecture is 12,992 satellites — roughly 6,080 between 500 and 600 km and 6,912 near 1,145 km — with ITU spectrum filings made in late 2020 under the designation GW. Chinese accounts describe a bus able to carry broadband, laser-communication, synthetic-aperture-radar and optical remote-sensing payloads rather than a single communications payload, which is why analysts read Guowang as strategic national infrastructure and not only as a consumer broadband service. What is not published is the part an operator would most want: no mass, no dimensions, no power budget and no capability description has been released for any Guowang flight, so treat any specific capability claim about an individual spacecraft as unsourced. This one flies in the near-polar shell, which China publishes as 86.5 degrees inclination at about 1,175 km.

A Zhuhai-1 (珠海一号) satellite, owned by Zhuhai Orbita Aerospace Science & Technology — in 2017 the first private Chinese company to launch and operate its own constellation. The planned constellation was 34 microsatellites of five payload types, and two of those types flew in quantity. The OHS hyperspectral satellites are the notable ones: 67 kg spacecraft at 500 km returning 10 m ground sample distance across a swath of more than 150 km and strips up to 2,500 km long, with 32 bands selectable by the user out of a 256-band capability spanning 400 to 1,000 nm at about 2.5 nm spectral resolution — a spectral–spatial combination that was genuinely unusual for a smallsat. The OVS video satellites stare rather than sweep, the first pair returning 1.98 m imagery over an 8 by 6 km scene and the OVS-2 generation 0.9 m at 25 frames per second for up to two minutes. The orbits differ by batch: the first video pair went to about 530 km at 43 degrees inclination, which is not sun-synchronous, while the later batches fly near 500 km at 98 degrees with 11:00 and 13:00 descending nodes. One limitation matters for any quantitative use: the hyperspectral satellites carry no on-board calibration device, which the operator's own co-authored literature acknowledges makes accurate calibration difficult. Orbita lists counter-terrorism among the constellation's markets; no named analyst has published a military assessment of it.

A ChinaSat (中星, Zhongxing) geostationary communications satellite operated by China Satcom, the state-owned commercial satellite operator, mostly built by CAST on the DFH-3, DFH-4 and DFH-4E platforms. The fleet does the ordinary work of a national GEO operator: television and radio distribution, VSAT and enterprise networks, maritime and aviation broadband, and disaster-relief connectivity, with China Satcom publishing the orbital slots — ChinaSat 19 at 163 degrees east, 10 and 10R at 110.5 degrees east, 12 at 87.5 degrees east, 26 and 6D at 125 degrees east, 6E at 115.5 degrees east. One caution belongs on every card in this family. ChinaSat is also the public designation under which the People's Liberation Army flies part of its own geostationary communications: J. Michael Dahm of the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, drawing on RAND's work, assesses that the Fenghuo ("beacon-fire") tactical series and the Shentong ("divine communication") strategic series fly as ChinaSat-1A, 1C, 20A, 2A, 2C and 2D. Those specific spacecraft are described separately in this catalogue where they appear; the rest of the ChinaSat fleet is commercial, and this site does not treat a shared brand as evidence about an individual satellite. Note also that the US Department of Defense's China Military Power Report names no ChinaSat at all — anyone citing the Pentagon for a specific spacecraft is over-reading it.

A 2,500 kg Space Test Program host at geostationary orbit, built by Northrop Grumman on a bus originally procured by DARPA for its Phoenix servicing programme and later transferred to STP. Its best-known passenger is NASA's Laser Communications Relay Demonstration, two 10 cm optical telescopes cross-connected by a switching unit so the satellite works as a genuine relay; it carried the first two-way end-to-end optical relay link with the ISS terminal ILLUMA-T at 1.2 Gbit/s in December 2023. Also aboard is an operational NNSA nuclear-detonation detection payload, plus AFRL, NRL and Air Force Academy space-environment sensors. A spacecraft can be owned and operated by one organisation and still carry, or be contracted to serve, another organisation's mission. Operated by U.S. Space Force Space Test Program, this spacecraft also carries a payload for the Laser Communications Relay Demonstration (LCRD), sponsored by NASA. NASA states plainly that this is a hosted payload aboard a U.S. Space Force spacecraft: a host does not have to be commercial for the mission to belong to somebody other than the spacecraft's owner. Published by NASA. It also carries a payload for UVSC Pathfinder, sponsored by NASA and the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory. The same spacecraft carries a second, unrelated science payload, which is why one satellite can appear under more than one programme here. Published by NASA.

A Shiyan (试验, shìyàn — "test" or "trial", not 实验 "experiment", which is how English references usually mis-render it) spacecraft. Nearly every Shiyan launch is announced by Xinhua with one formulaic sentence: the satellite is "mainly used for space environment detection and related technology tests." No operator is ever named, no payload is described, and no builder is identified in most cases — though the series demonstrably comes from many different organisations, including CAST, the Shanghai Academy of Spaceflight Technology, the Chinese Academy of Sciences' microsatellite institute and the Harbin Institute of Technology. The US Air Force's China Aerospace Studies Institute assesses Shiyan as the early stage of China's space technology pipeline, where new payloads are piloted on a common bus; SpaceNews assesses that individual flights have spanned technology demonstration, space environment monitoring, electronic intelligence, remote sensing, space situational awareness and rendezvous and proximity operations. That is an unusually wide span, and it is the reason this site names no mission for a Shiyan spacecraft: the family label is a classification marker, not a description. The formula is not universal, which is itself informative — Shiyan-19 was announced as land resource survey and urban planning, and the Shiyan-30 satellites as Earth-observation technology verification.

A satellite in the Geely Future Mobility Constellation (吉利未来出行星座), branded GEESATCOM — the only large orbital constellation owned by a carmaker. It is designed, built and operated by Geespace, formally Zhejiang Spacetime Daoyu Technology, the commercial space arm of the private Chinese automaker Geely; the company has since taken about 2 billion yuan from three Zhejiang and Hangzhou state investment vehicles, so "private" is the ownership and not the whole funding picture. Note that the operator's own account of the payload has changed: the 2022 launches were announced as centimetre-level positioning augmentation for autonomous driving, while the 2025 announcements describe a narrowband satellite messaging service carrying text, voice clips and images at up to 1,900 bytes per message, covering 60 degrees north to 60 degrees south and rated for 20 million users. Both descriptions are Geely's own words at different dates, and no independent source resolves which is flying. Phase I was declared complete in 2025 at 64 satellites against a 72-satellite plan, with later phases filed for 6,012. No named analyst and no US government listing associates Geespace with the Chinese military. It sits in the constellation's single published shell — about 600 km at 50 degrees inclination — which Geespace fills one orbital plane per launch, so an object's launch group is effectively its plane.

A Wideband Global SATCOM spacecraft: the high-capacity X- and Ka-band backbone of United States military satellite communications, and the system that replaced DSCS. Australia bought the sixth satellite into the constellation and a partner group of allies uses it alongside US forces. A spacecraft can be owned and operated by one organisation and still carry, or be contracted to serve, another organisation's mission. Operated by U.S. Space Force, this spacecraft also carries the Global Broadcast Service (GBS) on an allocated share of its own payload, sponsored by the Global Broadcast Service Joint Program, led by the U.S. Space Force. There is no separate broadcast box on these spacecraft: the fact sheet records an allocation of four of the satellite's own transponders to the broadcast service, which is a different programme with its own users, its own ground sites and its own budget line. Published by U.S. Space Systems Command. It also is part of the Wideband Global SATCOM international partnership, which partner nations funded and share access to, sponsored by Canada, Denmark, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and New Zealand, jointly with the United States. The manufacturer records that five countries funded this spacecraft together with the United States, and that it also serves Australia, which paid for a different one. Published by Boeing, the spacecraft's manufacturer.

A GPS satellite. NAVSTAR is the Global Positioning System's own programme designation, which is why the best-known constellation in orbit is catalogued under a name most people never see. The U.S. Space Force's 2nd Space Operations Squadron flies it as at least 24 slots in six equally spaced orbital planes at about 20,200 km, each satellite circling the Earth twice a day, with several extra spacecraft aloft so that coverage survives maintenance and decommissioning. For a maritime operator the point to hold onto is that this is a one-way broadcast of very weak signals from 20,000 km away: it is jammable and spoofable close to a contested coast, and most of what separates one satellite generation from the next is the effort to answer that. Block IIR — “replenishment”, built by Lockheed Martin and launched between 1997 and 2004 — carries the legacy signals only: the civil C/A code on L1 and the encrypted military P(Y) code on L1 and L2, with on-board clock monitoring and a 7.5-year design life. This one is Block IIR flight 9, space vehicle number SVN 45, last assigned pseudo-random-noise code PRN 21 in plane D, slot 3 of the constellation. It was retired on 27 January 2025 and boosted into a disposal orbit — which its own elements show, sitting roughly 800 km above the operational shell on a period some 34 minutes longer than a working GPS satellite's.

Fengyun-4C (风云四号C星), the third flight unit of China's second-generation geostationary weather satellite series — and, because space-track has misspelt the name as FENGYUNG, the one Chinese operational meteorological satellite that the site's Fengyun rule does not reach. It was launched on 26 December 2025 on a Long March 3B, is built by the Shanghai Academy of Spaceflight Technology and operated by the National Satellite Meteorological Centre, and is stationed at 133 degrees east, covering from 68 degrees east to 162 degrees west — China, the western Pacific and the Asia-Pacific. The payload is the reason a forecaster cares: the Advanced Geostationary Radiation Imager, now nineteen channels across visible, near-infrared, shortwave, mid-wave and thermal infrared; the Geostationary Interferometric Infrared Sounder, which is the capability the American GOES series does not have — a hyperspectral sounder in geostationary orbit returning temperature and humidity profiles continuously rather than twice a day from a polar orbiter; and a Lightning Mapping Imager. It also carries a solar and space-environment package, and the WMO records the mission as making a substantial contribution to space weather. It is a WMO-registered operational meteorological satellite, so unlike most spacecraft in this partition its data is part of the international exchange.

A Shijian (实践, shíjiàn — "practice", in the sense of putting something into practice) spacecraft. The catalogue also files this family under the abbreviation SJ. Fifty have launched since 1971, and it is the single most misread family in the Chinese catalogue, because it genuinely contains both ends of the spectrum: Shijian-10 was a recoverable microgravity and life-science capsule that ran 472 experiments for the Chinese Academy of Sciences, Shijian-13 flies commercially as ChinaSat-16 carrying twenty-six Ka-band beams for China Satcom, and Shijian-17, -21 and -25 have conducted the geostationary proximity operations that US Space Command has publicly described as a counterspace concern. The US Air Force's China Aerospace Studies Institute assesses that Shijian sits later in China's development pipeline than Shiyan — establishing operational practice for systems already adopted, rather than piloting new ones. Xinhua's standard announcement is that a Shijian satellite is "mainly used for space environment detection and related technology verification"; the Jamestown Foundation assesses the programme as deliberately dual-use and treats the absence of published operational data as itself indicative. This site names no mission for the family as a whole, because the family does not have one.

One of the five satellites of the Gaosu Jiguang Zuanshi Xingzuo Shiyan Xitong (高速激光钻石星座试验系统) — the "High-Speed Laser Diamond Constellation Test System" — launched together on 12 December 2024 from Jiuquan. The name is not Gaojing or Gaofen and these are not imaging satellites. Xinhua, CCTV and CASC all announced the system by name and confirmed that five satellites reached their planned orbits, and that is the entire official record: no mission statement, no payload, no builder. CASC named the Shanghai Academy of Spaceflight Technology as the builder of the rocket and its upper stage, and pointedly not of the satellites. SpaceNews assesses from the designation alone that the focus is inter-satellite laser communication links, which would matter for China because laser crosslinks reduce the dependence on overseas ground stations that China does not have. The launch put the five into three different orbital shells at 59.9 degrees inclination — one near 990 by 1,160 km, one near 790 by 810 km, and three near 975 by 990 km — using the upper stage's first three-orbit deployment, which is itself consistent with a link-geometry experiment. A satellite bus and manufacturer circulate in tracking databases; no Chinese source confirms either, and this site does not repeat them as fact.

A Chuangxin (创新, chuàngxīn — "innovation") spacecraft. The name has two distinct meanings in this catalogue and it is worth knowing which you are looking at. The original line is a genuine Chinese Academy of Sciences programme: Chuangxin-1, launched in 2003 at 88 kg, was China's first indigenous satellite under 100 kg, a UHF store-and-forward relay built to collect hydrological, meteorological, power-supply and disaster-relief data from remote unattended ground stations and dump it on a later pass. Its chief scientist published the specification in the Academy's own bulletin, and the Shanghai microsatellite institute that later became the CAS Innovation Academy for Microsatellites dates its founding to that launch. The second meaning is a naming convention rather than a programme: Chuangxin numbers are also used by the manufacturer as secondary designations for satellites announced publicly under other names — the Shiyan-6 spacecraft are also CX-3A, several Yaogan-30 triplets are also CX-5, and the Chuangxin-19 and Chuangxin-20 satellites in this catalogue are the same spacecraft as the satellite-internet test satellites catalogued elsewhere as HJS-3A and HJS-2A/B/C. So a Chuangxin designation tells you which institute built the spacecraft, and not necessarily what it does.

A geostationary satellite of SES, the Luxembourg operator that flies the largest combined GEO and MEO commercial fleet — around 120 spacecraft carrying video distribution and data connectivity for broadcasters, network operators, airlines, shipping and more than sixty governments. SES describes itself as the only commercial operator running a proven medium-Earth-orbit constellation alongside a geostationary fleet, and it absorbed Intelsat in 2025, so much of the world's commercial C- and Ku-band GEO capacity now sits under one operator. For a maritime or expeditionary user this is the ordinary commercial layer that carries reachback when a military system is saturated or out of footprint. A spacecraft can be owned and operated by one organisation and still carry, or be contracted to serve, another organisation's mission. Operated by SES, this spacecraft also carried a payload for the Commercially Hosted Infrared Payload (CHIRP), sponsored by the U.S. Air Force Space and Missile Systems Center. The sensor rode as a guest on a commercial telecommunications satellite and was decommissioned in December 2013 after 27 months of operation; the host spacecraft continues its own commercial mission. Published by the U.S. Office of Space Commerce. This arrangement has ended.

A Tianhui (天绘, "sky drawing") spacecraft — China's military mapping series, and one where the assessment is unusually well grounded. The WMO's own OSCAR database records the programme as dual-use with the People's Liberation Army responsible for the overall programme and its operations and CAST responsible for development, and states that imagery is downlinked to stations in China managed by the PLA. The China Space Report identifies the operating body as the China Tianhui Satellite Centre, a department under the Navigation and Survey Bureau of the Central Military Commission's Joint Staff Department. The generations differ in kind: Tianhui-1 flies a three-line-array stereo camera at 5 m with a 2 m panchromatic channel and 10 m multispectral on a 60 km swath, and its operating institute has published 1:50,000 mapping accuracy of about 10 m horizontal and 6 m vertical without ground control points; Tianhui-2 is China's first bistatic interferometric SAR formation, two X-band spacecraft at 3 m flying together to produce digital surface models; the Tianhui-4, -5, -6 and -7 payloads have never been disclosed at all. The satellites use sun-synchronous orbits with a 13:30 equator crossing and are replaced in sequence about six months before end of life.

One of the two Shiyan-12 spacecraft, launched together in December 2021 into geostationary orbit and built by CAST at about 3,000 kg each; CASC named its Fifth Academy as the builder and described them with the standard formula, "mainly used for space environment detection and related technology tests." Their observed behaviour is what makes them notable, and it is documented by commercial space-tracking firms rather than by any government. In February 2022 the pair manoeuvred away from an approaching US inspector satellite and turned to observe it — COMSPOC's research director characterised it as getting out of the way to avoid disclosing capability. In June 2024 Shiyan-12 01 closed to within about 75 km of a US military satellite under solar lighting favourable for imaging, and in September 2025 Shiyan-12 02 approached a US missile-warning spacecraft to about 60 km. Analysts therefore assess these as geostationary inspector satellites. No Chinese source says so, and this site does not present the assessment as a Chinese statement. Worth carrying alongside it: the Secure World Foundation's standing caution that none of China's rendezvous-and-proximity programmes has strong evidence linking it to co-orbital anti-satellite testing.

Three of India's Ku-band communications satellites double as the space segment of GAGAN, the GPS Aided GEO Augmented Navigation system, broadcasting in the L1 and L5 bands. GAGAN is India's satellite-based augmentation system: it transmits GPS corrections and integrity messages so that civil aviation and other precision users over the Indian region get better accuracy and, more importantly, a prompt warning when a GPS signal should not be trusted. ISRO records GSAT-15 as the third satellite to carry the GAGAN payload after GSAT-8 and GSAT-10, which were already providing navigation services from orbit. A spacecraft can be owned and operated by one organisation and still carry, or be contracted to serve, another organisation's mission. Operated by ISRO, this spacecraft also carries a payload for GPS Aided GEO Augmented Navigation (GAGAN), sponsored by the Airports Authority of India, jointly with ISRO. This is the case where owner and host are the same organisation and the mission still belongs to somebody else: ISRO built and flies the spacecraft, and states that the navigation signal is available through these two, but the service exists for the civil aviation authority. Published by the Indian Space Research Organisation.

A GPS satellite. NAVSTAR is the Global Positioning System's own programme designation, which is why the best-known constellation in orbit is catalogued under a name most people never see. The U.S. Space Force's 2nd Space Operations Squadron flies it as at least 24 slots in six equally spaced orbital planes at about 20,200 km, each satellite circling the Earth twice a day, with several extra spacecraft aloft so that coverage survives maintenance and decommissioning. For a maritime operator the point to hold onto is that this is a one-way broadcast of very weak signals from 20,000 km away: it is jammable and spoofable close to a contested coast, and most of what separates one satellite generation from the next is the effort to answer that. Block IIF — “follow-on”, built by Boeing and launched between 2010 and 2016 — added the third civil signal on L5, inside a protected aeronautical radionavigation band, together with advanced atomic clocks and a 12-year design life. This one is Block IIF flight 1, space vehicle number SVN 62, broadcasting pseudo-random-noise code PRN 25 in plane B, slot 2 of the constellation. It is the first Block IIF spacecraft, and so the first GPS satellite to broadcast the L5 civil signal operationally.

A satellite in SuperView Neo (高景, Gaojing, "high vista"), the second generation of China's commercial very-high-resolution imaging constellation. The spacecraft are built by CAST and owned by China Siwei Survey and Mapping Technology, a direct subsidiary of CASC, China's state prime space contractor — the constellation is sold commercially and owned by the state. The plan is 28 satellites: 16 optical at 0.2–0.3 m, four wide-swath at 0.7 m over a 100 km field, and eight synthetic-aperture radar at 0.5 m. The SuperView Neo-1 spacecraft carry a 0.3 m panchromatic and 1.2 m four-band multispectral imager on a 12 km swath from a 500 km sun-synchronous orbit with a 10:30 equator crossing; the SuperView Neo-2 spacecraft carry an X-band SAR instead, which is what makes them relevant to a maritime watch — the WMO rates that radar a primary instrument for sea-ice concentration and for oil-spill cover, both of which optical imagery cannot deliver through weather or darkness. The operator markets the constellation for maritime and security applications in its own materials. No named analyst has published a military attribution for SuperView; the dual-use reading here rests on the documented CASC ownership, not on anybody's assessment.

A Ludi Tance (陆地探测, "land exploration") radar satellite, also designated L-SAR. These are large spacecraft — over three tonnes, with a deployable antenna of more than 33 square metres — carrying L-band synthetic aperture radar. The band is the point: L-band's long wavelength penetrates vegetation canopy and dry soil where X-band and C-band radar do not, and it maintains interferometric coherence over long intervals, which is what makes it the band of choice for measuring slow ground deformation. The stated applications are land subsidence, landslide and earthquake deformation monitoring, infrastructure stability and geological survey, and the satellites fly as an interferometric pair. One note on the evidence: the programme name is associated with Earth observation, but this object flies a 1436-minute period at 15° inclination, 35,774-35,801 km, in geostationary orbit. Earth-imaging spacecraft overwhelmingly fly low, high-inclination or sun-synchronous orbits. The Earth observation that does happen from geostationary orbit is nearly all meteorological, which this taxonomy files under the separate 'weather' mission. The site records the programme attribution and notes the inconsistency rather than resolving it.

A Ziyuan (资源, "resource") spacecraft, China's civil land-resources imaging programme, with data distributed by CRESDA — a member of the international Committee on Earth Observation Satellites, though it records ZY data access as constrained rather than open. The programme has distinct branches and the catalogue name says which. ZY-1 spacecraft are the China–Brazil Earth Resources line: ZY-1 02D and 02E fly a 2.5 m panchromatic and 10 m eight-band multispectral imager on a 115 km swath plus a 166-band hyperspectral instrument at 30 m on 60 km, from a 778 km sun-synchronous orbit with a 10:30 descending node and a 26-day repeat, and 02E adds a 16 m thermal infrared camera at 8–10 μm. ZY-3 spacecraft are China's civil stereo mapping satellites, managed by the Satellite Surveying and Mapping Application Centre, carrying a three-line-array panchromatic camera — one telescope at nadir and one each tilted 22 degrees forward and back — at 2.1 m nadir and 2.6 m off-nadir on a 51 km swath, plus a 5.8 m four-band multispectral camera that covers the globe in about two months. Gunter Krebs notes that the Ziyuan programme also has a military branch, ZY-2, operated by the PLA; no ZY-2 spacecraft is in this catalogue.

CFOSAT, the China–France Oceanography Satellite — a joint CNSA and CNES mission and the most operationally consequential science spacecraft in this partition for anyone who forecasts sea state. It carries two radars that were designed to work together. SCAT is a rotating fan-beam Ku-band scatterometer at 13.256 GHz measuring ocean surface wind vectors across a swath of more than 1,000 km, specified at 2 m/s in speed and 20 degrees in direction. SWIM is the novel one: a real-aperture radar sweeping six beams from nadir out to 10 degrees incidence, which measures the directional spectrum of the waves themselves — not just significant wave height but which way the energy is running and at what wavelength, between about 70 and 500 m, over a 180 km swath. Measuring wind and directional wave spectra from the same platform at the same time is what makes the mission distinctive, because it constrains the wind-wave coupling that wave models have to assume. The data is in operational use in the West: since February 2021 CFOSAT directional wave spectra have been assimilated into Météo-France's operational MFWAM wave model, and SHOM, the French naval hydrographic service, is among the mission's partners.

A geostationary satellite of SES, the Luxembourg operator that flies the largest combined GEO and MEO commercial fleet — around 120 spacecraft carrying video distribution and data connectivity for broadcasters, network operators, airlines, shipping and more than sixty governments. SES describes itself as the only commercial operator running a proven medium-Earth-orbit constellation alongside a geostationary fleet, and it absorbed Intelsat in 2025, so much of the world's commercial C- and Ku-band GEO capacity now sits under one operator. For a maritime or expeditionary user this is the ordinary commercial layer that carries reachback when a military system is saturated or out of footprint. A spacecraft can be owned and operated by one organisation and still carry, or be contracted to serve, another organisation's mission. Operated by SES, this spacecraft also carries a payload for Global-scale Observations of the Limb and Disk (GOLD), sponsored by NASA. NASA bought a seat rather than a spacecraft: the instrument looks at Earth's upper atmosphere from a commercial telecommunications satellite whose owner also sells television and data capacity from the same orbital slot. Published by NASA.

A PIESAT-2 (Hongtu-2, 宏图二号) commercial radar satellite. Like the PIESAT-1 group before it, it flies as part of a four-satellite interferometric formation — one hub spacecraft transmitting and three auxiliaries receiving in a hub-and-spoke arrangement — so that a single radar transaction is observed from four slightly different positions at once. That is what lets the group measure surface height and surface movement rather than only imaging: the PIESAT-1 formation is quoted at 0.5 m in spotlight mode, mapping better than 1:50,000 globally within a year, with deformation sensitivity of 3 to 5 mm per year. The radar is X-band at 9.65 GHz. The spacecraft are owned by Zhuzhou Space Interstellar Satellite Technology and built by Shanghai Aerospace Technology, controlled by the state-owned Shanghai Academy of Spaceflight Technology; the operator plans sixteen radar satellites and markets the data commercially, with the Belt and Road region named as a target market. They fly sun-synchronous orbits near 520–530 km with a morning descending node. Reconnaissance use is asserted for this constellation only in unattributed form, and this site does not record an unattributed adverb as an assessment.

QZS-3, the geostationary member of the original four-satellite Michibiki constellation. Beyond positioning it carries Japan's satellite-based augmentation broadcast: since April 2020 the SBAS signal generated by the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism has been transmitted from a geostationary QZS rather than from the retired MTSAT spacecraft, giving aircraft range-error corrections and satellite-anomaly warnings over Japanese airspace. A spacecraft can be owned and operated by one organisation and still carry, or be contracted to serve, another organisation's mission. Operated by Cabinet Office of Japan (QZSS), this spacecraft also carries the Japanese satellite-based augmentation service (MSAS) on an allocated share of its own payload, sponsored by Japan's Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism. The Cabinet Office's own table shows the augmentation signal on exactly the two geostationary satellites of the constellation and on none of the four in quasi-zenith orbits, and states that the transport ministry produces the augmentation signal contents - one spacecraft, two ministries, two services. Published by the Cabinet Office, Government of Japan.

The registry lists this object only as "PAYLOAD C", but COSPAR 2013-037C is Shijian-15, named at that designation in Gunter Krebs's catalogue, which records SAST as the contractor and the reported mission as observation of space debris. It is the manoeuvring member of the three Chinese spacecraft launched together on 19 July 2013. The Secure World Foundation assesses that Shijian-15 carried the rendezvous and proximity capability and used it against Chuangxin-3, its co-passenger, in August 2013, again in April 2014, and again in May 2016 — and specifically that Shiyan-7, the satellite in the trio that carried a robotic arm, was not the spacecraft that performed the approach. That distinction matters, because the widely-repeated version of this story has the arm satellite grabbing another. Jonathan McDowell's contemporaneous reading was that Shijian-15 was observing debris while Chuangxin-3 may have served as a target for arm testing; Gregory Kulacki of the Union of Concerned Scientists noted that the Chinese-language announcements described debris observation, manipulator operations and space maintenance technology, and read the mission as possibly experimental debris collection.

This one is GPS III flight 9, named “Ellison Onizuka”, space vehicle number SVN 82, broadcasting pseudo-random-noise code PRN 20 in plane F, slot 5 of the constellation. An Intelsat geostationary communications satellite. Intelsat began in 1964 as the International Telecommunications Satellite Organization, an intergovernmental consortium that owned the world's first commercial international satellite network; it was privatised in 2001 and merged into SES in 2025, and the registry still records the fleet under the old ITSO code. The spacecraft carry C- and Ku-band capacity for broadcasters, telecom carriers, aeronautical and maritime networks, and a substantial share of US and allied government traffic bought commercially. The Epic series — designations ending in E, such as Intelsat 32e and 37e — are the high-throughput spot-beam generation. A spacecraft can be owned and operated by one organisation and still carry, or be contracted to serve, another organisation's mission. Operated by Intelsat, this spacecraft also carried a payload for Internet Routing In Space (IRIS), sponsored by the U.S. Department of Defense. The router was the first flown on a commercial geostationary satellite; the defence demonstration concluded in 2010 and the payload passed to commercial use. Published by Cisco, the payload's builder. This arrangement has ended.

One of ten Ningxia-1 (宁夏一号) radio-frequency monitoring smallsats, owned by Ningxia Jingui Information Technology — a four-employee company in Zhongwei — and built by DFH Satellite, a subsidiary of the state prime contractor CAST. What the payload does is stated by a Chinese government body: the Office of the Ningxia Radio Regulatory Committee describes using the Ningxia-1 satellites, with Zhongwei municipal government and the owner, to build an integrated space-and-ground radio spectrum monitoring network. Western reference works describe the same spacecraft as a signals-intelligence system, but every one of them hedges it — "have been reported to be" — without naming who reported it, so this site records the Chinese regulator's stated purpose and notes the SIGINT characterisation as unattributed rather than promoting it to an assessment. Ten were launched in two batches of five, in November 2019 and July 2021, into 45-degree orbits near 860 km; the second batch also carries the name Zhuzhou-1, a second municipal sponsor. Nothing has been published about the payload's bands, sensitivity or geolocation capability, and no further launches have followed since 2021.

A Zhangheng-1 spacecraft (张衡一号, also designated CSES, the China Seismo-Electromagnetic Satellite) — named for the Han dynasty polymath who built the first seismoscope in AD 132. It is a joint Chinese and Italian mission, with the Italian Space Agency and INFN contributing instruments, and it carries nine payloads for measuring the near-Earth electromagnetic and plasma environment: a Langmuir probe, an electric field detector, two magnetometers, a plasma analyser, energetic particle detectors and a GNSS radio occultation receiver. The mission's headline hypothesis is contentious — that earthquakes may leave detectable ionospheric or electromagnetic precursors — and the operator-side literature is appropriately careful, describing the data as valuable for studies of space weather, seismic events and the ionospheric environment rather than claiming prediction. For a space weather audience the earthquake question is beside the point: this is a well-instrumented ionospheric monitor in a 500 km sun-synchronous orbit, and its Italian investigators state that the data also supports study of coronal mass ejections, solar flares and the solar modulation of cosmic rays.

South Korea's first combined civil and military communications satellite, flown jointly by KT Corporation and the Agency for Defense Development; the military half is designated ANASIS 1, for Army/Navy/Air Force Satellite Information System. Alongside civil Ku- and C-band capacity it carries SHF transponders reserved for the armed forces, which is where the ROK military first got sovereign satellite communications rather than leased or allied capacity. A solar-array drive failure in 2013 crippled much of its capacity and led to an insurance claim. A spacecraft can be owned and operated by one organisation and still carry, or be contracted to serve, another organisation's mission. Operated by KT Corporation / Agency for Defense Development, this spacecraft also shares its bus with the Korean military satellite communications (ANASIS-1) payload, sponsored by the Republic of Korea Agency for Defense Development. The spacecraft was built as South Korea's first combined civil and military communications satellite; a drive mechanism failure in 2013 reduced its capacity, and public sources do not say what remains in service. Published by Gunter's Space Page.

A Taijing (泰景) commercial remote-sensing satellite built and operated by MinoSpace, a Beijing smallsat manufacturer that is both developer and user of this line. The number after the name identifies the class rather than the flight order: Taijing-1 and Taijing-2 are small optical imagers on the MN50 bus, Taijing-3 is a larger optical satellite of about 240 kg imaging at around half a metre on the MN200S bus, and Taijing-4 carries an X-band synthetic aperture radar with a phased-array antenna more than five metres across, working in sliding-spotlight and stripmap modes at up to one metre. The four spacecraft in this catalogue all flew together on one Kinetica-1 launch from Jiuquan in January 2024. Several Taijing satellites carry a second, sponsor-derived Chinese name — a common arrangement in China's commercial sector, where an organisation buys naming rights to a flight. No named analyst has published a military assessment of this constellation. One transaction is worth knowing about: Gunter Krebs records that a different spacecraft in the line, Taijing-3 04, was reportedly transferred on orbit to a Russian company and now operates as Stilsat 1.

Hellas-Sat 3 is a condominium spacecraft at 39° East: one satellite carrying two owners' payloads. The Ku-band mission belongs to Hellas Sat, an Arabsat subsidiary, and replaced Hellas-Sat 2's direct-to-home and telecom services across Europe, the Middle East and southern Africa with more than double the transponder count; the S-band payload belongs to Inmarsat and is the space segment of the European Aviation Network. Shared spacecraft like this are common at contested orbital slots, and they are the reason a single catalogue number can have two operators with two entirely different missions. A spacecraft can be owned and operated by one organisation and still carry, or be contracted to serve, another organisation's mission. Operated by Hellas Sat / Inmarsat, this spacecraft also shares its bus with the the European Aviation Network (EAN) payload, sponsored by Inmarsat, now part of Viasat. This is a condominium satellite: two operators bought one spacecraft together, one taking the S-band payload and the other more than forty Ku-band transponders, and the registry can record only one of them as the owner. Published by Gunter's Space Page.

Haiyang-4A, launched 13 November 2024 and announced by China as the ocean salinity detection satellite (海洋盐度探测卫星). Sea surface salinity is the hardest of the ocean-surface variables to measure from orbit — the brightness-temperature signal is small and sits at L-band, so it needs a large aperture — and China's stated purpose is to fill its own gap in high-accuracy global salinity measurement. It carries two microwave payloads: an interferometric microwave radiometer, which synthesises the aperture rather than flying one, and MICAP, a combined active and passive microwave imager whose radar channel corrects the passive measurement for surface roughness. CNSA names the user departments — the Ministry of Natural Resources, the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs, the Ministry of Emergency Management and the China Meteorological Administration — and names ocean environment forecasting, ecological forecasting, water-cycle monitoring, short-term climate prediction and global climate change research as the applications, with soil moisture as a secondary product. It flies a 654 km sun-synchronous dawn-dusk orbit with a 06:00 descending node.

ASO-S, the Advanced Space-based Solar Observatory, known in China as Kuafu-1 (夸父一号) after the giant who chased the sun. Launched 9 October 2022 into a 720 km sun-synchronous orbit at 98.2 degrees — a dawn-dusk orbit gives near-continuous view of the Sun — it is China's first comprehensive solar observatory and its science goal is summarised as "one magnetism, two eruptions": the magnetic field, and the two kinds of eruption that field drives. The Full-disc vector MagnetoGraph measures the photospheric magnetic field; the Lyman-alpha Solar Telescope images the disc and inner corona in Lyman-alpha and white light to catch coronal mass ejections as they leave; the Hard X-ray Imager images flare footpoints in hard X-rays. Observing the field and both eruption signatures at once is the point, because the open question is how stored magnetic energy converts into a flare and a CME. The mission states improving space weather forecast capability among its objectives, which for anyone tracking geomagnetic storms is the practical relevance: CMEs seen leaving the Sun here are the ones that arrive at Earth one to four days later.

Block IIR-M — “modernised”, launched between 2005 and 2009 — added the second civil signal L2C and the military M-code, the jam-resistant signal with flexible transmit power that makes GPS usable in an electronic-warfare environment. This one is Block IIR-M flight 5, space vehicle number SVN 57, broadcasting pseudo-random-noise code PRN 29 in plane C, slot 1 of the constellation.

A Tianping (天平, "balance" or "scales") calibration satellite. These are reference targets rather than sensors: a spacecraft whose radar cross-section and orbit are precisely known, flown so that ground radars and optical trackers can be calibrated against something whose true answer is already established. China's own announcement says so plainly — the satellite is used for calibration of ground-based radar equipment and radar cross-section measurement, supports imaging experiments for ground-based optical equipment, and contributes to low-orbit space environment monitoring and to correcting orbital prediction models. The programme runs from Tianping-1 in 2018 through Tianping-2 to the Tianping-3 group. Two things are worth an operator's attention. Calibration is inherently dual-use — the same reference improves a weather radar, a space surveillance radar and a target-detection radar — which SpaceNews notes without alleging anything further. And Chinese state media described the October 2024 Tianping-3 launch as carrying a single satellite while the manufacturer's own account and the catalogue both show three.
