The registry lists this object only as "PAYLOAD A", but it is identifiable: COSPAR 2013-037A is Shiyan-7, one of three Chinese spacecraft launched together on a Long March 4C from Taiyuan on 19 July 2013. Independent sources agree on the assignment — Gunter Krebs places Shijian-15 at 2013-037C and Chuangxin-3 at 2013-037B, leaving A, and satellite trackers name 39208 as Shiyan-7 directly. Shiyan-7 is the spacecraft in that trio reported to carry a teleoperated robotic arm for capturing other space objects, and the trio's manoeuvres that August became one of the most-analysed episodes in Chinese space activity. The Secure World Foundation's account is the careful one, and it cuts against the loudest version of the story: it assesses that Shijian-15 conducted the proximity operations against Chuangxin-3, and that Shiyan-7 — the satellite with the arm — was not the one involved. Anonymous US officials at the time described a covert anti-satellite programme; the Foundation flags that characterisation as speculation. Some catalogues carry this launch under a third set of names entirely, Tansuo-3, -4 and -5.

Michibiki No. 6, the first of the three satellites added to grow QZSS from four spacecraft to seven. The Cabinet Office confirmed it reached its operational geostationary position at about 90.5 degrees East in February 2025, well west of Japan, which pushes the reach of the system's signals across the Indian Ocean region rather than only over the home islands. A spacecraft can be owned and operated by one organisation and still carry, or be contracted to serve, another organisation's mission. Operated by Cabinet Office of Japan (QZSS), this spacecraft also carries the Japanese satellite-based augmentation service (MSAS) on an allocated share of its own payload, sponsored by Japan's Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism. The Cabinet Office's own table shows the augmentation signal on exactly the two geostationary satellites of the constellation and on none of the four in quasi-zenith orbits, and states that the transport ministry produces the augmentation signal contents - one spacecraft, two ministries, two services. Published by the Cabinet Office, Government of Japan.

A BRO (Breizh Reconnaissance Orbiter) satellite: Unseenlabs, a French company based in Rennes, flies these to detect and geolocate the radio-frequency emissions of ships at sea. The premise is that a vessel intent on not being seen can switch off its AIS transponder, but it cannot switch off everything — navigation radar, VHF, VSAT and the rest keep radiating — and each emitter has a signature that can be characterised and matched across passes. That gives a picture of what is on the water regardless of cloud, darkness or whether the vessel is cooperating, which is what AIS cannot do and what optical and SAR imaging can only do where they happen to be looking. Unseenlabs describes it as data that complements AIS, VMS, SAR and optical rather than replacing them, and that is the honest reading: RF geolocation tells you something is emitting from roughly there, and it takes a second sensor to say what it is. Each spacecraft is a smallsat carrying a single wide-band RF payload, so the constellation's revisit — not any one satellite — is the capability.

Yuxing-3 06 (驭星三号06星), also named Xiyuan-0 — China's first commercial experimental satellite carrying a flexible robotic arm, launched in March 2026 and built by Suzhou Sanyuan Aerospace, a subsidiary of Emposat, with Hunan University of Science and Technology. It exists to test the manipulation problem behind on-orbit servicing: simulated refuelling operations, force-compliant handling, and precision control of an arm that flexes rather than one that is rigid. Two points of precision matter. The refuelling was simulated, and no propellant transfer has been confirmed. And Victoria Samson of the Secure World Foundation, commenting publicly, was notably positive — not about any military capability but about the transparency, calling the level of detail in the company's statement impressive and arguing that sharing details of new on-orbit activities helps allay concerns about their ultimate purpose. That is the only on-record comment from a Western space-security analyst on this spacecraft, and it cuts the opposite way from the usual framing.

Shijian-21, launched October 2021 by SAST and announced by China as being "mainly used to test and verify space debris mitigation technologies." In January 2022 it did exactly that, and the demonstration was more capable than the announcement implied: ExoAnalytic Solutions observed it dock with the defunct BeiDou-2 G2 navigation satellite, execute a large burn that carried the dead spacecraft about 3,000 km above the geostationary belt into a graveyard orbit, and undock four days later. A spacecraft that can dock with an uncooperative satellite and move it can move a working one, which is why the demonstration drew attention — but the analysts closest to the data declined to characterise it as hostile. The Secure World Foundation's Victoria Samson said it could be read either way; CSIS's Todd Harrison said there were more questions than answers. In mid-2025 Shijian-21 conducted extended proximity operations with Shijian-25, the refuelling demonstrator, and the two became optically inseparable on 2 July before separating on 29 November.

DSN-1/Superbird-8, a dual-purpose spacecraft built by Mitsubishi Electric on its DS2000 platform. The Superbird-8 side carries Ku- and Ka-band capacity for SKY Perfect JSAT's commercial services in Japan, replacing the 18-year-old Superbird-B2 at 162 degrees East; riding with it is the X-band DSN-1 payload for Japan's Ministry of Defense. One spacecraft therefore carries both commercial capacity and an element of Japan's dedicated military X-band SATCOM. A spacecraft can be owned and operated by one organisation and still carry, or be contracted to serve, another organisation's mission. Operated by SKY Perfect JSAT / DSN Corporation, this spacecraft also shares its bus with the Japanese Ministry of Defense X-band satellite communications (DSN) payload, sponsored by the Japanese Ministry of Defense. The commercial Ku- and Ka-band payload and the defence X-band payload fly on the same spacecraft, and the company operating the commercial side is also the contractor running the military network. Published by Gunter's Space Page.

Shijian-17, a roughly 4,000 kg CAST spacecraft on the DFH-4S bus, launched November 2016 on the maiden flight of the Long March 5 and inserted directly into geostationary orbit. What it has done since is the reason it matters. In early 2018 AGI's ComSpOC logged it rendezvousing with ChinaSat-20 and then holding station for five weeks, generally under 10 km and several times inside 1 km; CSIS independently documented it traversing the geostationary belt from about 37.7 degrees east to 180 degrees east across that year. In April 2021 General James Dickinson, then commander of US Space Command, told the Senate Armed Services Committee that Shijian-17 carries a robotic arm and that space-based robotic arm technology could be used in a future system for grappling other satellites. That is a US military assessment on the record, not a Chinese statement, and China has never described the spacecraft's payload. Free manoeuvre across the geostationary belt is itself the significant capability here, independent of what the arm is for.

Shijian-25, launched January 2025, and unusual in this partition because its builder said plainly what it is for. The Shanghai Academy of Spaceflight Technology states that the satellite's main mission is to validate the technology for satellite refuelling and life extension. From July 2025 it conducted extended rendezvous and proximity operations with Shijian-21 in geostationary orbit, becoming optically inseparable from it on 2 July and separating again on 29 November. Whether propellant actually transferred is not established by anybody: COMSPOC set out three scenarios — a successful docking, a deliberate rehearsal without docking, or an aborted final approach — and Slingshot Aerospace called its own data inconclusive, noting that any docking lasted no more than three hours. Two US satellites repositioned to watch, which Jonathan McDowell described as very unusual and previously undocumented. Treat the widely-repeated figure for how much propellant was transferred as unsourced; nobody has published evidence for it.

A spacecraft in China's Yaogan series, assessed by the U.S. Department of Defense as People's Liberation Army intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance. This attribution is contested: China characterises it as civil remote sensing for land surveys, crop-yield estimation and disaster relief, while the U.S. Department of Defense assesses it as military intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance. This site records the assessment by the U.S. Department of Defense and shows both readings. One note on the evidence: the programme name is associated with Earth observation, but this object flies a 1436-minute period at 3° inclination, 35,730-35,847 km, in geostationary orbit. Earth-imaging spacecraft overwhelmingly fly low, high-inclination or sun-synchronous orbits. The Earth observation that does happen from geostationary orbit is nearly all meteorological, which this taxonomy files under the separate 'weather' mission. The site records the programme attribution and notes the inconsistency rather than resolving it.

A Haiyang-1 (海洋一号, "ocean") spacecraft — the ocean-colour half of China's civil ocean observation programme, built by CAST and operated by the National Satellite Ocean Application Service under the Ministry of Natural Resources. The primary instrument is COCTS, the China Ocean Colour and Temperature Scanner: ten channels, eight narrow visible and near-infrared bands from 412 to 865 nm plus two thermal channels at 11 and 12 μm, 1.1 km at nadir across a swath widened to 2,900 km on HY-1C and HY-1D, giving daily global coverage. Alongside it fly a 50 m coastal zone imager on a 950 km swath for red tide, green tide, sea ice and pollution, an ultraviolet imager that exists to correct the atmosphere over turbid near-shore water, and an AIS receiver — ship position reporting on an ocean-colour satellite is a stated function, not an inference. HY-1C and HY-1D deliberately fly as a morning and afternoon pair, 10:30 descending and 13:30 ascending, which doubles the chance of a cloud-free look at the same water in a day.

A UHF Follow-On spacecraft. The UFO constellation carried the U.S. Navy's narrowband tactical satellite communications from geostationary orbit, serving ships, submarines and aircraft, and is being replaced by the Mobile User Objective System. A spacecraft can be owned and operated by one organisation and still carry, or be contracted to serve, another organisation's mission. Operated by U.S. Navy, this spacecraft also carries a payload for the Global Broadcast Service (GBS), sponsored by the Global Broadcast Service Joint Program, led by the U.S. Space Force. These U.S. Navy ultra-high-frequency communications satellites were modified during construction to carry an additional Ka-band broadcast package for a different service run by a different part of the department; the U.S. Space Force fact sheet records that the broadcast service used payloads on two such satellites without naming which, so the site lists the three that were built with the payload and does not pick two. Published by Gunter's Space Page.

A Tiantong-1 (天通一号) geostationary mobile satellite communications spacecraft — China's own S-band mobile satellite service, and the system that lets a Chinese handset work beyond terrestrial coverage without a foreign operator. It is built by CAST on the DFH-4 platform with a large deployable mesh reflector, which is what makes a handheld-sized terminal possible: the aperture has to be on the satellite because it cannot be on the phone. The service covers China, its surrounding seas and, with successive spacecraft, a wider swathe of Asia, Africa and the Pacific, and it is used for maritime, aviation, emergency response and disaster relief. Sources disagree on the operating entity — Gunter's Space Page records China Satcom, satellite databases record China Telecom, and the distinction is between the satellite operator and the service provider. Strategic value is inherent rather than assessed: sovereign mobile satellite service means Chinese users are not dependent on Inmarsat or Iridium.

Xinzhengcheng-01 (新征程01卫星, "New Journey-01"), a technology-demonstration microsatellite from the CAS Satellite Technology Group, flown on the maiden launch of the Kinetica-2 rocket in March 2026. Its operator describes it as a miniature space laboratory: a smart cabin with a viewport, carrying commercial off-the-shelf equipment for in-orbit trials, with cameras inside and outside. Two details deserve care. The operator's own wording changed between releases — an earlier factory-review announcement called the payload a space surveillance camera, while the launch-day release called it a remote-sensing camera; both are the operator's words, no outside analyst has commented on the difference, and this site records it as a wording change rather than as evidence. Separately, the Chinese space-tracking firm SpaceMapper reports that in April 2026 this satellite took part in a long-range approach and safe-withdrawal test with Xinzhengcheng-02, the cargo spacecraft prototype it launched with.

One of the two Ludi Tance 1-01 (陆地探测一号01组) spacecraft, also written Lutan-1 — China's first civil L-band differential interferometric SAR constellation, built by the Shanghai Academy of Spaceflight Technology with the Ministry of Natural Resources as lead user. The two satellites launched a month apart in early 2022 and fly as a formation in a quasi-sun-synchronous orbit near 607 km. Two things make this system distinctive. L-band's long wavelength penetrates vegetation and dry soil and holds interferometric coherence over long intervals, which is what makes it the band of choice for measuring slow ground deformation. And in its first phase the pair operate bistatically, with a separation between 700 and 7,000 m, so that a single pass yields an interferogram — normally that requires two passes days apart, with all the atmospheric and coherence problems that brings. CNSA names land and resource management, earthquakes, disaster mitigation, surveying and forestry as the applications.

A Tianlian (天链, "sky link") data relay satellite — China's equivalent of the American TDRS system, and the reason Chinese crewed missions can talk to the ground almost continuously. A spacecraft in low Earth orbit is in sight of any one ground station for only a few minutes per pass; a relay satellite in geostationary orbit can see it for most of an orbit and pass its traffic down to a single site. Tianlian-1 established the capability from 2008 and made continuous coverage of the Shenzhou missions possible; Tianlian-2 is the second generation, on a larger CAST platform with greater capacity. The users are China's crewed spaceflight programme, the space station, and low-orbiting spacecraft needing high-rate downlink or real-time command — which necessarily includes both civil and military satellites, since the relay serves whoever is assigned to it. Relay satellites are strategic infrastructure in any country's inventory, and China publishes little about the traffic these carry.

Haishao-1 (海哨一号, "Sea Sentinel-1"), China's first synthetic aperture radar satellite designed for ultra-low Earth orbit — around 350 km, well below where imaging satellites normally fly. The trade is deliberate: flying lower means the radar sees a stronger return for a given antenna and power, so the same resolution can be had from a much smaller spacecraft, and this payload is under 80 kg while returning sub-metre X-band multi-polarisation imagery. The cost is drag, which is why very low orbits are hard to hold. It was built by the Chinese Academy of Sciences' Qilu Aerospace Information Research Institute and launched in December 2024. The Chinese-language release from the institute is more specific than the English one about what it is for, and names ocean environment observation of Hainan and the South China Sea and maritime target monitoring among its roles — a declared maritime surveillance function, stated by the operator rather than assessed by anyone.

The US catalogue's placeholder name for China's reusable experimental spacecraft (可重复使用试验航天器), an uncrewed spaceplane launched on a Long March 2F and returned to a runway. China has published no name, no dimensions, no mass and no images; the name "Shenlong" that circulates widely was coined by Chinese space enthusiasts and is not official. Xinhua's announcement said only that the spacecraft would conduct technological verification for reusable spacecraft, providing technical support for the peaceful use of space. What is on the record is the flight history — a two-day flight in 2020, then missions of 276 and 266 days — and the behaviour: on more than one mission the spacecraft has released and in some cases recaptured a small companion object, with commercial trackers including LeoLabs detecting them. The obvious comparison is the US Space Force's X-37B, and the obvious caution is that neither government has said what either vehicle carries.

Optus and Defence C1 is one geostationary spacecraft carrying two payloads for two owners: commercial Ku-band services for Optus, and UHF, X- and Ka-band military communications for the Australian Department of Defence. It was built under a contract placed by Optus and the Department jointly, and the site records it as mixed rather than military for that reason. A spacecraft can be owned and operated by one organisation and still carry, or be contracted to serve, another organisation's mission. Operated by Optus / Australian Department of Defence, this spacecraft also shares its bus with the Australian Defence Force satellite communications on Optus C1 payload, sponsored by the Australian Department of Defence. One spacecraft carries commercial television capacity in one frequency band and military communications in three others, and the commercial operator holds the prime contract for the military side. Published by Gunter's Space Page.

A spacecraft in China's Yaogan series, assessed by the U.S. Department of Defense as People's Liberation Army intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance. This attribution is contested: China characterises it as civil remote sensing for land surveys, crop-yield estimation and disaster relief, while the U.S. Department of Defense assesses it as military intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance. This site records the assessment by the U.S. Department of Defense and shows both readings. One note on the evidence: the programme name is associated with Earth observation, but this object flies a 271-minute period at 20° inclination, 7,490-7,504 km, in medium Earth orbit. Imaging missions overwhelmingly use low, high-inclination or sun-synchronous orbits. Medium Earth orbit is where navigation constellations fly; it is not an imaging orbit. The site records the programme attribution and notes the inconsistency rather than resolving it.

DAMPE, the Dark Matter Particle Explorer, known in China as Wukong (悟空) after the Monkey King — the name is a pun, since the character's defining ability is seeing what is really there. It is a high-energy particle telescope in a roughly 500 km sun-synchronous orbit, built around a plastic scintillator detector, a silicon-tungsten tracker, a deep BGO calorimeter and a neutron detector, and it measures cosmic-ray electrons and positrons, gamma rays and cosmic-ray nuclei with better energy resolution than anything flown before it in its band. Its best-known result, published in Nature in 2017, was the direct detection of a spectral break in the cosmic-ray electron-plus-positron spectrum at about 0.9 TeV across a measured range of 25 GeV to 4.6 TeV — a feature that constrains both nearby astrophysical accelerators and dark matter annihilation models. It is a pure science mission with no military or dual-use dimension claimed by anyone.

A Wideband Global SATCOM spacecraft: the high-capacity X- and Ka-band backbone of United States military satellite communications, and the system that replaced DSCS. Australia bought the sixth satellite into the constellation and a partner group of allies uses it alongside US forces. A spacecraft can be owned and operated by one organisation and still carry, or be contracted to serve, another organisation's mission. Operated by U.S. Space Force, this spacecraft also carries the Global Broadcast Service (GBS) on an allocated share of its own payload, sponsored by the Global Broadcast Service Joint Program, led by the U.S. Space Force. There is no separate broadcast box on these spacecraft: the fact sheet records an allocation of four of the satellite's own transponders to the broadcast service, which is a different programme with its own users, its own ground sites and its own budget line. Published by U.S. Space Systems Command.

The registry lists this object only as "PAYLOAD B", but COSPAR 2013-037B is Chuangxin-3, identified by that designation in Gunter Krebs's catalogue, which also records the orbit as 666 by 672 km at 98.06 degrees — a match for this object. Chuangxin-3 is a small store-and-forward communications satellite developed by the Chinese Academy of Sciences with the Shanghai Academy of Spaceflight Technology and Shanghai Telecom, in the same line as Chuangxin-1: it collects short data messages from unattended ground stations and relays them on a later pass. It is also the passive party in a well-known episode. The Secure World Foundation assesses that in August 2013 Shijian-15, launched alongside it, conducted rendezvous and proximity operations against Chuangxin-3 to within a few kilometres, repeating the exercise in April 2014 and May 2016 — so this modest communications spacecraft has spent much of its life as somebody else's target.

Catalogued under a Jianbing designation, this is Ziyuan-2 03 — the third of China's Ziyuan-2 imaging satellites, launched in November 2004 and built by CAST. Jianbing (尖兵, "vanguard") is the internal Chinese designation series for reconnaissance satellites, and it is secret: only the public Yaogan and Ziyuan numbers are officially used, so a Jianbing number appearing in a catalogue is itself a signal about how the object is understood outside China. Gunter Krebs assesses that Ziyuan-2, though reported as a civil Earth-observation system, was code-named Jianbing-3 and was China's first high-resolution military imaging satellite, used for area surveillance; Chinese officials denied a military mission for Ziyuan-2 in October 2000. The claim that US intelligence identified it as an exclusively military photo-reconnaissance satellite rests on unnamed sources, and this site records it as such rather than as a government finding.

A Zhihui Tianwang-1 (智慧天网一号, "Smart SkyNet-1") spacecraft — China's first medium Earth orbit broadband communications satellites, launched as a pair in May 2024 into an orbit near 20,000 km. The concept came from Tsinghua University and the spacecraft were built by the Shanghai Academy of Spaceflight Technology, which describes satellite A as the technology validation spacecraft, carrying a multi-beam high-speed microwave link, a two-way laser inter-satellite link and an on-board digital processing and forwarding platform, with satellite B carrying a supporting laser link experiment payload. MEO is a deliberate middle choice: far fewer satellites are needed for global coverage than in low orbit, and latency is far lower than geostationary. The declared applications are networking with China's Antarctic and Arctic stations, ocean shipping, aircraft, and low-orbiting remote-sensing satellites needing a relay.

Tansuo-1 (探索一号), also designated Shiyan-1 — a 204 kg spacecraft launched in April 2004 and China's first transmission-type small satellite able to do stereo terrain mapping, meaning it downlinked digital imagery directly rather than returning film. It was designed jointly by the Harbin Institute of Technology, the Chinese Research Institute of Space Technology, the CAS Changchun Institute of Optics and the Xi'an Surveys and Designs Institute, and was officially described as being for land resource photographic survey, geographic environment monitoring and mapping research. Gunter Krebs adds the assessment that matters historically: although a civil remote-sensing satellite, its digital imaging capability was important for proving technology for a new generation of Chinese military reconnaissance spacecraft then under development. Note it is not a Tsinghua satellite, an attribution that circulates widely.

A polar-orbiting communications satellite relaying mobile voice and data through Iridium's cross-linked global constellation. A spacecraft can be owned and operated by one organisation and still carry, or be contracted to serve, another organisation's mission. Operated by Iridium Communications, this spacecraft also carries a payload for Aireon space-based aircraft surveillance (Aireon), sponsored by Aireon LLC, founded by Iridium with five national air navigation service providers and wholly owned by Iridium since July 2026. Aireon states that the aircraft-tracking receivers are built into each satellite of this constellation, which is why an entire commercial telephone network doubles as air-traffic surveillance infrastructure; the original 1990s satellites of the same name never carried them, which is why this claim is attached to catalog numbers rather than to the word Iridium. Published by Aireon.

Assessed to be a Nivelir-L satellite inspector. This is the most operationally interesting class in the Russian catalogue and also the least documented: Russia announces nothing beyond a Kosmos number, and the identification rests on what the object then does. Each of these three was launched into a plane matching an American reconnaissance satellite -- Kosmos 2576 into the plane of the KH-11 USA 314 in May 2024, and Kosmos 2588 into the plane of USA 338 in May 2025, both measured and published by Marco Langbroek from optical tracking. Earlier members of the family deployed subsatellites of their own, one of which US officials said displayed the characteristics of a space-based anti-satellite weapon. Krebs marks his own programme attribution with a question mark, and this site keeps that uncertainty: what is measured is the orbital behaviour, and what is inferred from it is the mission.

An Air Force Research Laboratory subsatellite released near the geostationary belt by EAGLE, the ESPA Augmented Geosynchronous Laboratory Experiment flown on the AFSPC-11 mission. The catalogue records only a USA designation and the analysts disagree. It flies just below geostationary altitude, so it drifts steadily eastward against the belt rather than holding a slot. This attribution is contested: Jonathan McDowell (planet4589.org GCAT) characterises it as ESPASat 1 - an AFRL ESPA-class experimental subsatellite; McDowell places Mycroft on catalogue entry 43465 (2018-036G, USA 287) instead, while Gunter Krebs (Gunter's Space Page) assesses it as Mycroft - an AFRL inspector satellite built to manoeuvre around and image the EAGLE host; Krebs marks the USA 285 identification as tentative. This site records the assessment by Gunter Krebs (Gunter's Space Page) and shows both readings.

A Xingchi-1 (星池一号, "Star Pool-1") satellite from the Chinese commercial operator EllipSpace — the first networking pair of a constellation the company plans to grow past a hundred spacecraft. The two flew together on a Long March 2C in December 2023 as rideshares with Egypt's MisrSat-2. The operator's description is unusually specific about on-board autonomy rather than optics: the satellites carry several types of remote-sensing payload and are built for wide-field guided imaging, high-precision in-orbit geolocation and target extraction from the imagery, autonomous mission planning, high-speed parallel computation on board, and deep in-orbit reconfiguration of the satellite's own functions. Extracting targets on the spacecraft rather than on the ground is the significant claim there, because it changes what has to be downlinked and how quickly a result can be delivered.

One half of a Tianhui-2 bistatic radar pair — China's first close-formation interferometric SAR system. The two spacecraft are identical, fly in slightly different orbits so that their separation traces a controlled baseline, and share one radar transaction: one transmits, both receive. That geometry measures height directly from the phase difference between the two returns, which is how a radar mission produces a digital surface model rather than an image. The system works in X-band at about 3 m resolution from a 500 km sun-synchronous orbit and is described by its Chinese engineering literature as able to produce global digital surface models and radar orthophotos in a short time. Like the rest of the Tianhui series it is assessed as PLA-operated — by the WMO's OSCAR database, by Gunter Krebs and by the China Space Report — rather than declared as such by China.

A Xingyun (行云, "running cloud") narrowband satellite Internet-of-Things demonstrator, the low-Earth-orbit machine-to-machine project of CASIC — the state-owned aerospace and defence conglomerate that is the sibling of CASC. The intended service is the same class as Tianqi: short data messages relayed from unattended sensors, containers, vessels and pipelines in places with no terrestrial network, with laser inter-satellite links tested on the Xingyun-2 pair. What an operator should know is the lineage rather than the payload: J. Michael Dahm of the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory records that the Xingyun project is led by CASIC's Fourth Academy, which developed ballistic missile technology for the People's Liberation Army. That is a statement about the organisation, not about what these two spacecraft do, and this site does not convert one into the other.

Assessed to be a Lotos-S1 (14F145) electronic intelligence satellite -- the operational half of Russia's Liana system, built by KB Arsenal and flown under Kosmos numbers that conceal which programme each flight belongs to. Lotos-S1 listens rather than looks: it locates and characterises radars and radio transmitters on land, and it pairs with the radar-carrying Pion-NKS satellites that do the same job against ships. The whole series flies the same circular orbit, about 900 km up at 67.1 degrees, which is the strongest single clue that ties an unlabelled Kosmos number to this programme; RussianSpaceWeb and Gunter Krebs both number the flights 802 onward and agree with each other. For an operator this is the Russian counterpart to a national SIGINT constellation, and its revisit over any given emitter is set by that orbit, not by anything Russia has published.

A Hulianwang Gaogui (互联网高轨卫星, "high orbit internet satellite") spacecraft — a Ka-band very-high-throughput geostationary communications satellite built by CAST. Beware the translation: in Chinese usage "high orbit" means anything above low Earth orbit, so these are ordinary geostationary satellites and not high Earth orbit spacecraft. They are the geostationary complement to China's low-orbit broadband effort, and Jonathan McDowell placed the first of them in context immediately as the Chinese equivalent of ViaSat-3 or Jupiter-3. Xinhua reported before the first launch that the system would provide coverage for the whole of China and for key areas along the Belt and Road. CASC did not disclose the payload before launch and revealed the satellite's name only in the success announcement afterwards; Gunter's Space Page marks even the operator as uncertain.

The Hard X-ray Modulation Telescope, named Insight in English and Huiyan (慧眼, "wise eyes") in Chinese — China's first X-ray astronomy satellite, operated by the Institute of High Energy Physics. It carries three collimated instruments covering low, medium and high energy X-rays out to a few hundred keV, and it uses direct demodulation of a scanning collimator rather than focusing optics, which gives it a very large collecting area at hard X-ray energies at the cost of imaging resolution. It surveys the Galactic plane, monitors black hole and neutron star binaries through outbursts, and has contributed to gamma-ray burst and gravitational-wave follow-up. The operator's own pages disagree slightly on the high-energy band, giving 20–250 keV in one place and 20–350 keV in another; that is a documentation inconsistency, not a dispute about the instrument.

Lingqiao (灵巧通信试验卫星, the "Smart Communications Test Satellite"), China's first low Earth orbit mobile communications satellite — a roughly 130 kg spacecraft launched in September 2014 from a project begun in 2010 by Tsinghua University with Xinwei Telecom. It demonstrated on-board smart antennas, on-board processing and switching, and integrated space-ground networking, and Tsinghua's account lists the services it proved: calls between handheld satellite terminals, calls between a handheld satellite terminal and an ordinary mobile phone, internet data transfer — and electromagnetic spectrum monitoring and geolocation, which is a signals-collection capability declared by the operator itself rather than assessed by an outside analyst. It should not be confused with the Lingqiao Video satellites in this catalogue, which are Jilin-1 imaging spacecraft.

Beijing-1, a 166 kg microsatellite built in the United Kingdom by Surrey Satellite Technology on the SSTL-150 platform for Beijing Landview Mapping Information Technology, and launched in October 2005. It was the fifth spacecraft of the first-generation Disaster Monitoring Constellation — an international arrangement in which several countries each owned one compatible satellite and shared imaging capacity for disaster response. It carries two instruments: a 4 m panchromatic imager, and a 32 m multispectral imager with an unusually wide 600 km swath, the combination giving both detail and the coverage rate that disaster response needs. One note on the catalogue name: the "(TSINGHUA)" in the registry string is unexplained, no source establishes any Tsinghua University role in this spacecraft, and Beijing-1 is a different satellite from Tsinghua-1.

Taiji-1 (太极一号), catalogued under the launch designation KX-09 — China's first technology-verification satellite for space-based gravitational wave detection, launched August 2019 and built by DFH Satellite for the Chinese Academy of Sciences. Detecting gravitational waves from orbit means measuring changes in the separation of free-falling test masses far smaller than an atom, and everything about the spacecraft exists to make that measurement possible: a laser interferometer demonstrating displacement accuracy at the 100-picometre level, micro-thrusters controllable to better than a micronewton, and drag-free attitude control, in which the spacecraft flies itself around an internal test mass so that the mass feels nothing but gravity. The name is the Chinese term for the supreme ultimate, familiar in the West as the yin-yang symbol.

A Rassvet-3 satellite: the first operational generation of Bureau 1440's low-orbit broadband constellation, Russia's answer to Starlink and OneWeb. Bureau 1440 is a private company inside X Holding rather than a Roscosmos programme; it flew the experimental Rassvet-1 in 2023 and Rassvet-2 in 2024, and began launching operational batches of sixteen on Soyuz-2-1b from Plesetsk in March 2026, aiming at 288 satellites and commercial service in 2027. Each 370 kg spacecraft carries optical inter-satellite terminals, so traffic can cross the constellation without touching the ground -- the same architectural choice, and the same strategic consequence, as the Western systems it copies. Newly launched batches are still climbing: the spread of altitudes across these objects in the catalogue is orbit raising in progress, not a designed shell.

Assessed to be a Strela-3 military communications satellite. Kosmos is a designation rather than a programme -- Russia files most military spacecraft and many civil ones under it, so the number deliberately tells a reader nothing -- and the identification here comes from outside analysts reading the orbit, the launch manifest and the radio emissions. Strela-3 is a store-dump system: the satellite records a message as it passes over the sender, carries it, and replays it to a ground station later in the orbit. That buys global reach for units with no line of sight to a relay, at the cost of a delay measured in tens of minutes, and it is why these satellites fly in clusters of two or three in a 1,400-1,500 km, 82.5-degree plane. Gonets, the civil constellation flying in the same shell, is the civilian derivative of this system.

This object was launched by a Titan IV from Vandenberg on a National Reconnaissance Office ocean-surveillance mission: a second-generation Parcae, or NOSS, cluster whose satellites locate ships and aircraft by triangulating their radio emissions. The catalogue records only a USA designation, and analysts disagree over which catalogued object is which. This attribution is contested: Jonathan McDowell (planet4589.org GCAT) characterises it as SLDCOM 4 - the Titan Launch Dispenser that deployed the triplet, carrying a tuneable UHF relay payload; McDowell assigns USA 119 to a different catalogue entry (23862), while Gunter Krebs (Gunter's Space Page) assesses it as Parcae 13A - a second-generation NOSS ocean-surveillance subsatellite. This site records the assessment by Gunter Krebs (Gunter's Space Page) and shows both readings.

A Michibiki satellite of Japan's Quasi-Zenith Satellite System, the regional positioning system the Cabinet Office operates to complement GPS. Most members fly the north-south asymmetric figure-of-eight quasi-zenith orbit that parks a satellite high over Japan for the greater part of each day, because a signal arriving from near the zenith is the one that urban canyons and mountains do not block; the constellation has been operated as a four-satellite system since November 2018, with three satellites always visible from the Asia-Oceania region. QZS-2 and QZS-4 are two of the quasi-zenith-orbit members. For a positioning user in the western Pacific this means more satellites at usable elevation and, through the sub-metre and centimetre-level augmentation signals the same spacecraft broadcast, better accuracy than GPS alone.

Assessed to be a Tundra (14F142) spacecraft of the EKS or Kupol early-warning system -- the Russian counterpart to the American SBIRS, watching for the infrared plume of a ballistic missile launch. The orbit is the whole design: a twelve-hour Molniya ellipse inclined near 63 degrees, apogee close to 39,000 km over the northern hemisphere, so that each satellite loiters for hours over the polar approaches where a geostationary satellite sees only a grazing edge. EKS replaced the Soviet Oko network, which had lapsed entirely by 2014, and analysts have identified the flights as Tundra 11L through 16L. For a watch officer the practical point is that these satellites are the sensor behind Russian launch-detection timelines, and that their coverage is a function of a known orbit rather than of anything Russia publishes.

A Weina (微纳, "micro-nano") nanosatellite. This is one of the genuine unknowns in the catalogue and this site is not going to invent a mission for it. China named the spacecraft in its launch announcements and said nothing whatever about what it does; Gunter Krebs, the most complete public reference for Chinese spacecraft, records the series as being of unknown purpose and unknown configuration, and reports only that it is believed to belong to the Shanghai Micro Satellite Engineering Center. All three flew as secondary payloads alongside Yaogan reconnaissance satellites. One caution matters here, because it is the easy mistake: the mission statements published for those Yaogan launches — electromagnetic environment detection, for instance — describe the primary payload, not the Weina spacecraft riding with it.

An ION Satellite Carrier: not a free-flying payload but an orbital transfer vehicle - a tug - built and flown by the Italian company D-Orbit. Customers' satellites ride inside a modular 64U dispenser and ION releases them one at a time, changing altitude and local time of the ascending node between deployments so that each spacecraft is dropped into its own slot, or so that a whole constellation batch is phased along a plane in weeks rather than months. Once the deployment phase ends the same vehicle becomes a hosting platform, running third-party payloads and edge-computing experiments for the rest of its life, so an ION in the catalogue is usually carrying other operators' hardware rather than a mission of its own. Each flight is given a mission name and the vehicle a personal name, following naval practice.

One of a group of four small military satellites launched together on an Angara-1.2 from Plesetsk and given consecutive Kosmos numbers -- 2591 to 2594 in August 2025, 2615 to 2618 in April 2026. RussianSpaceWeb lists the first group under the index 14F178 and the working name OO-MKA, and Gunter Krebs believes the type is optical reconnaissance, but he writes the attribution with a question mark and the sensor has never been described. What is solid is the pattern: four near-identical spacecraft per launch in a very low sun-synchronous orbit around 285-330 km, where drag is severe and orbital life is short. That is the signature of a proliferated imaging constellation flown cheaply and replaced often, rather than of a few exquisite satellites, and it is a change in how Russia is buying reconnaissance.

Luch (Olymp) 2, launched in March 2023, and the clearest case on this site of behaviour speaking louder than a designation. It shares a name with Russia's civil data-relay satellites but does not behave like one: the commercial space-tracking firm Slingshot Aerospace has repeatedly published its manoeuvres from slot to slot along the geostationary arc, parking within a few tenths of a degree of Western commercial communications satellites -- Eutelsat 3B and Intelsat among them -- for weeks at a time and then moving on. Its predecessor Olymp-K-1 did the same for years. The widely reported inference is that it is listening to the uplinks of the satellites it sits beside; Russia has never described the payload, so this card records the manoeuvres, which are measured, and not the mission, which is not.

Skykraft of Canberra is building the world's first full-service space-enabled air traffic management constellation, and these are its prototype and pre-production blocks - note that the catalog spells the later batch SKYCRAFT while the earlier ones are SKYKRAFT. Each satellite carries an ADS-B receiver to capture aircraft position reports and, unusually, a VHF payload that relays controller-pilot voice and data link communications directly between aircraft using their existing radios and the air navigation service provider. Skykraft demonstrated space-based VHF with Airservices Australia in 2023 and has an ITU filing accepted for a 2976-satellite system; the practical significance is closing the surveillance and communications gap over oceanic and remote airspace, which covers most of the planet.

An APSTAR geostationary communications satellite operated by APT Satellite Holdings of Hong Kong — a listed commercial operator serving Asia, the Middle East, Africa, Europe and Australia with television distribution, cellular backhaul, VSAT and maritime and aviation connectivity. The fleet is a mix of Chinese and Western manufacture. APSTAR-6D, at 134 degrees east, is the notable one: a high-throughput satellite with about 90 user beams and more than 50 Gbps of capacity, using Ku-band for the user beams and Ka-band for the gateway links — a distinction often reported wrongly as a Ka-band HTS. Note that the catalogue entry APSTAR 6E SPS is not a satellite in its own right: it is the separable propulsion system flown with APSTAR-6E, which detached after delivering the spacecraft to its slot.
